blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The standard error (SE) of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. For the mean of n independent observations, SE(x̄) = σ/√n, which is estimated from one sample by s/√n. For a proportion, SE(p̂) = √[p(1 − p)/n], estimated by √[p̂(1 − p̂)/n].

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Recall §6.5: Var(x̄) = σ²/n. The SE is its square root, σ/√n: the typical distance between a sample mean and the population mean. You never know σ, so you plug in the sample SD, s. That is why a single sample is enough to estimate how much its own mean would wobble across repeated samples. For a proportion, recall that a 0/1 (Bernoulli) variable has variance p(1 − p) (§5.7.1.1); putting σ² = p(1 − p) into σ²/n gives the SE of a proportion.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: For the 30 children seen at the under-five clinic today (recall §1.4), the mean weight is 11.81 kg and s = 1.75 kg.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Estimated SE = s/√n = 1.75 ÷ √30 = 1.75 ÷ 5.477 = 0.32 kg.
  2. Meaning: over repeated samples of 30 from the same population, sample means would typically lie about 0.32 kg from the true mean.
  3. Two independent sample means differ from each other by more: the SE of their difference is √2 × 0.32 ≈ 0.45 kg (rule 3 of §6.5: the variances add).
  4. Checking the EPI 30×7 design (recall §6.2.6). Take the worst case p = 0.5, which makes p(1 − p) largest. With n = 210 children at DEFF = 2, the effective sample size is 210 ÷ 2 = 105. SE = √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 105) = 0.049. A 95% margin is 1.96 × 0.049 = 0.096, about ±10 percentage points, as the design promises. The 1.96 is the z value that cuts off the central 95% of the Normal curve (recall §5.7.2.2.1); §7.2 builds confidence intervals on it.

points.html: SE is not SD. The SD describes the spread of individual values; the SE describes the spread of a statistic over repeated samples. SE = SD/√n is always smaller for n > 1, so reporting “mean ± SE” as a description of the sample makes the data look far less variable than they are. In one audit of four anaesthesia journals, 198 of 860 articles (23%) used the SE inappropriately to describe sample variability (Nagele, 2003). Describe data with the SD; describe the precision of an estimate with the SE or a confidence interval.
SE shrinks with √n, not n. Doubling n multiplies the SE by 1/√2 ≈ 0.71; halving the SE needs four times the sample.
For cluster samples the SRS formula understates the SE: multiply it by DEFT = √DEFF (§6.2.6). In the CBHI survey, 0.021 becomes 0.032 (0.0205 × 1.56 before rounding).
The SE is the building block of confidence intervals (§7.2) and of most test statistics (Chapters 8–10).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 6.4

questions.prompt: A colleague doubles her sample size and expects her standard error to halve. Is she right? What sample-size multiple would halve it?
questions.answer: No. SE = σ/√n, so doubling n multiplies the SE by 1/√2 = 0.71: a 29% reduction, not 50%. To halve the SE, √n must double, so n must be multiplied by 4.

questions.prompt: If the clinic survey weighed 120 children instead of 30 and the SD stayed at 1.75 kg, what would the estimated SE of the mean be?
questions.answer: SE = 1.75 ÷ √120 = 1.75 ÷ 10.95 = 0.16 kg. This is half the SE for 30 children (0.32 kg), as expected for four times the sample.

questions.prompt: Using the rule “variances of independent variables add”, show that Var(x̄) = σ²/n. Then state what the Law of Large Numbers adds, and what the Central Limit Theorem adds beyond it.
questions.answer: x̄ = (X₁ + … + Xₙ)/n with independent Xᵢ each of variance σ². Var(X₁ + … + Xₙ) = σ² + … + σ² = nσ² (variances add for independent variables). Var(x̄) = (1/n)² × nσ² = σ²/n (a constant factor c scales the variance by c²). Because E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n shrinks to 0, x̄ settles at μ as n grows: that is the Law of Large Numbers. The LLN says where x̄ ends up; the CLT adds the shape of its sampling distribution for large n, approximately Normal with mean μ and SD σ/√n, whatever the population’s shape. That shape is what allows Normal-based confidence intervals and tests.
